entry: American paralegal and environmental activist. As a legal clerk for attorney Ed Masry, Brockovich helped build a 1993 case against Pacific Gas & Electric Company (PG&E) over [[Groundwater|groundwater]] contamination in Hinkley, California. The case settled in 1996 for $333 million, the largest settlement ever paid in a direct-action lawsuit in United States history to that date. It inspired the Oscar-winning film *Erin Brockovich* (2000), starring [[Julia Roberts]]. Critics argue that the film overstated the causal link between the contamination and widespread illness.

Most massive known dwarf planet in the Solar System. Eris is a [[Trans-Neptunian object|trans-Neptunian object]] in the scattered disk, with a highly eccentric orbit. It was discovered in January 2005 by a team led by Mike Brown and named in September 2006 after the Greco-Roman goddess of strife and discord. Eris is 2,326 ± 12 km in diameter, and its mass is 27% greater than that of [[Pluto]], although Pluto is slightly larger by volume. In February 2016 it was 96.3 AU from the Sun, more than three times the distance of [[Neptune]]. Its apparent size led the International Astronomical Union to define the term planet in 2006, classing [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]], Pluto and Eris as dwarf planets. Eris has one large confirmed moon, Dysnomia.

Country in the [[Horn of Africa]] on the Red Sea coast (pop., 2026: about 3.7 million). It is a unitary presidential republic with its capital at [[Asmara]], bordering [[Ethiopia]], [[Sudan]] and [[Djibouti]]. The [[Kingdom of Aksum]], centered in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, was established in the first or second century AD. Italy formed the colony of Italian Eritrea in 1889. Ethiopia annexed Eritrea in 1962, and Eritrea gained de facto independence in 1991 and de jure independence in 1993 after a referendum. Isaias Afwerki has been president since independence. The People's Front for Democracy and Justice is the sole legal party, and national legislative and presidential elections have never been held. The human rights record has been described as among the worst in the world; the government dismisses such allegations as politically motivated.

American film and television actor. Borgnine won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Marty* (1955), which also won Best Picture. He starred as the title character in the sitcom *McHale's Navy* (1962–1966) and served in the U.S. Navy during [[World War II]]. He voiced Mermaid Man in *SpongeBob SquarePants* from 1999 until his death. At age 92 he earned a Primetime Emmy Award nomination for the 2009 series finale of [[ER (TV series)|ER]].

American novelist, short-story writer and journalist. His economical, understated prose influenced later 20th-century writers. Hemingway wrote seven novels, six short-story collections and two non-fiction works, several of which are classics of American literature. He served as an ambulance driver on the [[Italian front (World War I)|Italian front]] and was seriously wounded in 1918. In Paris in the 1920s he was associated with the expatriate [[Lost Generation]] community; his debut novel, *The Sun Also Rises* (1926), followed. *A Farewell to Arms* (1929) drew on his war experience. He covered the [[Spanish Civil War]] for *For Whom the Bell Tolls* (1940). *The Old Man and the Sea* (1952) won the [[Pulitzer Prize]] for Fiction, and he was awarded the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature. Injuries from two plane crashes in Africa in 1954 left him in pain and ill health for much of the rest of his life.

American physicist and Nobel laureate. Lawrence received the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing the [[Particle accelerator|cyclotron]], a circular accelerator with a chamber set between the poles of an electromagnet. He joined the [[University of California, Berkeley]], in 1928 and became its youngest full professor two years later. His Radiation Laboratory built a series of ever larger cyclotrons. During World War II he developed electromagnetic isotope separation, using devices called calutrons, to enrich uranium for the [[Manhattan Project]]. He founded the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory was also named for him. Element 103, lawrencium, was named in his honor.

New Zealand physicist and chemist. Known as the father of nuclear physics, Rutherford received the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry "for his investigations into the disintegration of the elements, and the chemistry of radioactive substances." He named [[Alpha particle|alpha]] and beta radiation and, with Thomas Royds, showed that alpha radiation consists of [[Helium]] nuclei. In 1911 he proposed that an atom's charge is concentrated in a small nucleus, based on the gold foil experiment of Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden. In 1912 he invited [[Niels Bohr]] to his laboratory, which led to the [[Bohr model]] of the atom. In 1917 he performed the first artificially induced nuclear reaction and identified the [[Proton|proton]]. As director of the Cavendish Laboratory at the [[University of Cambridge]], he oversaw the 1932 discovery of the [[Neutron|neutron]] by James Chadwick. He was made a baron of the United Kingdom.

Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer. Shackleton first went to Antarctica in 1901 as third officer on [[Robert Falcon Scott]]'s Discovery expedition. On the Nimrod expedition (1907–1909), his party set a Farthest South record of 88°23′ S, only 97 geographical miles from the [[South Pole]]. On the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, his ship *Endurance* was trapped in pack ice in the [[Weddell Sea]] and sank in 1915. The crew camped on the ice, then reached Elephant Island by lifeboat, and Shackleton sailed 720 nautical miles to South Georgia to bring rescue. He died of a heart attack while his ship was moored at South Georgia on a 1921 expedition. Later rediscovered as a model of leadership in extreme circumstances, he was voted eleventh in a [[BBC]] poll of the 100 Greatest Britons.

German zoologist, naturalist and philosopher. Haeckel was professor of zoology at the University of Jena from 1862 to 1909 and promoted the work of [[Charles Darwin]] in Germany. He discovered, described and named thousands of new species and coined terms in biology, including [[Ecology|ecology]], [[Phylum|phylum]], phylogeny, ontogeny and [[Protist|Protista]]. His recapitulation theory, summed up as "ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny," is disproven but was influential. The embryo illustrations he used to support it were drawn incorrectly, and whether they were falsified or drawn poorly is debated. His *Kunstformen der Natur* (*Art Forms in Nature*) contains over 100 multicolor illustrations of sea creatures and animals, and it influenced [[Art Nouveau]]. Haeckel promoted scientific racism, endorsed [[Eugenics|eugenics]] and embraced Social Darwinism.

Austrian physicist and philosopher. Mach studied shock waves produced by projectiles moving faster than sound. With his son Ludwig, he used schlieren photography to photograph the shadows of invisible shock waves. The ratio of an object's speed to the speed of sound is named the [[Mach number]] in his honor. His criticism of [[Isaac Newton]]'s theories of space and time foreshadowed [[Albert Einstein]]'s [[Theory of relativity|theory of relativity]]. As a philosopher of science, he influenced [[Positivism|logical positivism]] and [[Pragmatism|American pragmatism]], defending a phenomenalism that recognized only sensations as real.

Multinational professional services network. EY, formerly Ernst & Young, provides assurance, tax, information technology, consulting and transaction services. It is one of the Big Four professional services firms, with [[Deloitte]], [[KPMG]] and [[PwC]]. The network is headquartered in [[London]], and approximately 406,000 people work in more than 700 offices in over 150 countries and territories. The firm was formed through a merger in 1989 and adopted the EY name in 2013. It has faced repeated scrutiny over its training, hiring and work culture.

Greek god of love and sex. In the earliest accounts Eros is a primordial god; in later accounts he is the son of [[Aphrodite]]. He is usually depicted as a winged youth with a bow and arrows that make mortals and gods fall in love. The Romans called him Cupid or Amor. His best-known myth is the story of Eros and Psyche. In Christian art of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, the putti and cherubim descended from his iconography, and the Cupid form became a symbol of Valentine's Day.

Consensual psychological humiliation used to produce [[Sexual arousal|sexual arousal]]. It occurs mainly within [[BDSM]] domination and submission activity, and also in pornography, webcam modeling and sexual roleplay. Relatively little has been written about it. Whether an act is humiliating depends on the shared interpretation of the participants rather than on the act itself. A 2015 study of 1,580 women involved in BDSM found that 66.77% enjoyed verbal humiliation and 77.53% enjoyed physical humiliation.

Sensual bodywork on erogenous zones for sexual pleasure or orgasm. Massage techniques are applied to erogenous zones to produce or enhance sexual arousal and sometimes [[Orgasm|orgasm]]. Erotic massage is sometimes part of sex as [[Foreplay|foreplay]], as the final sex act, or as sex therapy. A "happy ending" is the colloquial term for a massage that ends in sexual release, often a [[Handjob|handjob]]. In many jurisdictions it is regarded as a sexual service, and its legality varies; in some, erotic massage may be legal while [[Prostitution|prostitution]] is not.

Art, literature or photography that deals substantively with erotic subject matter. Erotic art may take any form, including painting, sculpture, drama, film or music. Some critics regard [[Pornography|pornography]] as a type of erotica; many consider them separate. Some have argued that pornography aims at the graphic depiction of sexual scenes, while erotica "seeks to tell a story that involves sexual themes." Erotic art dates back to Paleolithic cave paintings. Mass-market erotic photography found its roots in pornographic magazines, notably [[Playboy]], founded in the 1950s. The Sanskrit text the [[Kama Sutra]] is among the most iconic erotic literature.

Australian and American actor. Flynn was known for romantic swashbuckler roles, including [[Robin Hood]] in *The Adventures of Robin Hood* (1938) and the lead in *Captain Blood* (1935). He frequently co-starred with [[Olivia de Havilland]] and also starred in [[Western (genre)|Westerns]] such as *Dodge City* (1939). He was posthumously awarded two stars on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1960. In 1942 he was tried on three counts of [[Statutory rape|statutory rape]] involving two underage girls, and a jury acquitted him in February 1943.

Methods for reliable delivery of digital data over unreliable communication channels. Error detection identifies errors caused by noise during transmission, and error correction reconstructs the original data. Both add redundant check bits to a message. Common detecting codes include the parity bit and cyclic redundancy checks. Hamming codes correct errors; the (7,4) code uses three parity bits to correct single-bit errors in four data bits. Richard Hamming is credited with the modern development of error-correcting codes in 1947, and [[Claude Shannon]]'s work on [[Information theory|information theory]] set limits on error-free communication over noisy channels. Jewish scribes of the 7th to 10th centuries CE devised the Numerical Masorah to ensure accurate copying of the [[Hebrew Bible]].

Sigmoid special function, also called the Gauss error function. It is defined as erf(z) = (2/√π) ∫₀ᶻ e^(−t²) dt, and it occurs often in [[Probability|probability]], [[Statistics|statistics]] and [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]]. For a [[Normal distribution|normally distributed]] variable with mean 0 and standard deviation 1/2, erf(x) is the probability that the variable falls between −x and x. J. W. L. Glaisher named the function in 1871. It also arises in solutions of the [[Heat equation]] when boundary conditions follow the Heaviside step function.

Edible annual plant in the family [[Brassicaceae]]. Also called arugula or rocket, *Eruca sativa* is native to the Mediterranean and [[Asia]]. Its sharp, slightly bitter, peppery flavor makes it a popular leaf vegetable in salads. The plant grows 20 to 100 cm tall and has creamy white petals with purple veins. It prefers full sun, cool temperatures and moist, fertile soil, and hot weather changes its flavor. Raw arugula is 92% water and is a rich source of folate and vitamin K. As an [[Invasive species|invasive species]], it is prolific in the Sonoran desert of Arizona and California.

headword: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD
sort_key: eruption of mount vesuvius in 79 ad
entry: Volcanic eruption in [[Campania]], Italy. In 79 AD [[Mount Vesuvius]] ejected a cloud of tephra and gases to a height of 33 km, reaching the [[Stratosphere|stratosphere]]. The eruption released about 100,000 times the thermal energy of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It destroyed several Roman towns, including [[Pompeii]] and Herculaneum, which were buried under [[Pyroclastic flow|pyroclastic flows]] and ashfall. The two cities had a combined population of over 20,000, and the remains of over 1,500 people have been found there. The main firsthand account survives in two letters by Pliny the Younger, who watched from Misenum.

German field marshal during [[World War II]]. Rommel served in the [[Wehrmacht]] of Nazi Germany and commanded the 7th Panzer Division during the 1940 invasion of France. His leadership of German and Italian forces in North Africa earned him the nickname the Desert Fox. He had received the Pour le Mérite in [[World War I]] and published *Infantry Attacks*, a book on military tactics, in 1937. He commanded German forces opposing the Allied invasion of Normandy in June 1944. After he was implicated in the 20 July plot to assassinate [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]], he was given a choice between suicide and trial, and took a cyanide pill. Postwar accounts often portrayed him as an apolitical commander, a view other historians have called the "Rommel myth."

Austrian theoretical physicist. Schrödinger devised the [[Schrödinger equation|Schrödinger equation]], which calculates the wave function of a system and how it changes over time. He shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with [[Paul Dirac]] "for the discovery of new productive forms of atomic theory." He coined the term [[Quantum entanglement|quantum entanglement]] in 1935. His thought experiment [[Schrödinger's cat]] is his best-known idea in popular culture. He also wrote on [[Statistical mechanics]] and [[General relativity]], and in *What Is Life?* he addressed genetics from the standpoint of physics. He left Germany in 1933 because of the Nazis' antisemitism and held a position in [[Dublin]] until his retirement in 1955. In 1989 allegations of sexual abuse of several minors emerged; a 2026 defense challenged some of them.

American singer, songwriter and record producer. Badu was called the "Queen of Neo Soul" by critics after her debut album, *Baduizm* (1997), placed her at the forefront of the neo soul movement. The album was certified triple platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America and spawned the singles "On & On" and "Appletree." Her second album, *Mama's Gun* (2000), included the top 10 single "Bag Lady." Her voice has been compared to that of [[Billie Holiday]]. Badu has won five [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]] and has acted in films, including *The Cider House Rules*.

Four-carbon sugar alcohol used as a sweetener. Erythritol (C₄H₁₀O₄) occurs naturally in some fruits and fermented foods and is made commercially from corn using enzymes and [[Fermentation|fermentation]]. It is 60–70% as sweet as [[Sucrose|table sugar]] but almost completely noncaloric, and it does not affect blood sugar or cause [[Tooth decay|tooth decay]]. Japanese companies pioneered its use as a sweetener in the 1990s, and it is approved in more than 60 countries. About 80–90% of an oral dose is excreted unchanged in urine within 24 hours.

Minimum speed needed to escape a body's gravitational influence without further propulsion. In celestial mechanics, escape velocity is the speed at which a ballistic object escapes the orbit of a primary body, with no other forces or gravity-producing objects acting on it. For a spherically symmetric body of mass M, the escape speed at distance d from its center is vₑ = √(2GM/d), where G is the [[Gravitational constant|gravitational constant]]. For [[Earth]], escape velocity is 11.186 km/s. Rockets need not reach escape velocity in a single maneuver, and a [[Gravity assist|gravity assist]] can siphon kinetic energy from large bodies.
